examples.problem_statement: The difference between two numbers is 16. What can be said about the total numbers divisible by 7 that can lie in between these two numbers.

solution.result: at least 2 multiples of 7 always lie inside the gap
solution.description: Note that a gap of 16 always contains two multiples of 7, so the count is definitely at least two.

solution.result: the case that pushes the count to 3
solution.description: Take the first number in the form one less than a multiple of 7, since that placement squeezes an extra multiple into the interval.
Use the book's instance of that form: 27 is one less than 28, and adding the difference 16 gives the other number 43.
List the multiples of 7 lying between 27 and 43 to see this case yields three, not two.

examples.answer: may be 2 or 3 depending upon the numbers

key_reminders: A fixed difference of 16 guarantees two multiples of 7 in between, never fewer.
Starting the interval at a number of the form 7n - 1 is what admits a third multiple.
common_mistakes: Dividing 16 by 7 and answering a single fixed count of 2, missing the 7n - 1 starting position that gives 3.
Counting the endpoints themselves as numbers lying in between.

examples.problem_statement: If a is a multiple of 18 and b is a multiple of 12, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. (A) a - b is divisible by 6. (B) a + b is divisible by 12. (C) a \times b is divisible by 18. (D) a \div b is divisible by 6.

solution.result: prime factor sets for a and b
solution.description: Build a factor tree for each multiple so every guaranteed prime factor of a and of b is visible before testing any statement.

solution.result: both a and b are divisible by 6, so a - b is too; select (A)
solution.description: Check (A): 6 needs a 2 and a 3, and both a and b carry both, so each is a multiple of 6 and their difference is as well.

solution.result: 30 is not a multiple of 12; eliminate (B)
solution.description: Check (B): b is a multiple of 12 but a need not be, so test the counterexample a = 18, b = 12 and see the sum fails.

solution.result: contains a 2 and two 3s, so it is divisible by 18; select (C)
solution.description: Check (C): pool the prime factors of a and b, then confirm the pool contains the 2, 3, 3 that 18 requires.

solution.result: not even known to be an integer; eliminate (D)
solution.description: Check (D): dividing the factor sets leaves an unknown quotient, so divisibility by 6 cannot be guaranteed.

examples.answer: (A) a − b is divisible by 6; (C) a × b is divisible by 18

key_reminders: A multiple of n is guaranteed to carry every prime factor of n, and nothing more.
If two numbers are each divisible by d, their sum and difference are divisible by d.
The prime factors of a product include all prime factors of both operands.
common_mistakes: Assuming a is a multiple of 12 because b is, which wrongly validates (B).
Treating a \div b as an integer when nothing forces b to divide a, which wrongly validates (D).

concept.sub_category: Descriptive statistics: mean and standard deviation

examples.problem_statement: A list of numbers has a mean of 8 and a standard deviation of 2.5. If x is a number in the list that is 2 standard deviations above the mean, what is the value of x ?

solution.description: Read off the given mean and standard deviation and restate the position of x relative to the mean.
Convert the distance from standard-deviation units into actual units by multiplying 2 by the standard deviation 2.5.
Add that 5-unit distance to the mean of 8, since x lies above the mean.

key_reminders: A value k standard deviations above the mean equals mean + k \times (\text{standard deviation}).
Above the mean means add the distance; below the mean would subtract it.
common_mistakes: Adding 2 instead of (2)(2.5), giving 10 rather than 13.
Multiplying the mean by the standard deviation instead of offsetting it.
